content_html:
Conceptual thinking

Whilst conceptual thinking seems detached from external phenomena, it’s still anchored in embodied, spatial, and emotional schemata - the deep architecture of how memory gives shape to thought.

Even in the highest forms of abstract or conceptual thought (like mathematics, philosophy, or theoretical physics), memory and imagination rely on spatial, sensory, and metaphorical scaffolds that originate in embodied experience. Even when no external sensory object exists, the brain reuses the same neural systems it employs for perception and movement to simulate structure and relationship. For example, mathematicians often report that a proof “feels” like moving through a space, or that an equation has “shape” or “weight.” These aren’t poetic flourishes; they’re literal activations of parietal and occipital regions involved in spatial reasoning.

This is consistent with conceptual metaphor theory (Lakoff & Núñez, Where Mathematics Comes From, 2000), which argues that much of abstract reasoning is built upon image schemas - primitive spatial and bodily experiences (like containment, balance, path, source-goal) mapped onto abstract domains. The idea of mathematicians visualising rooms, colours, or spatial divisions to separate concepts is an extension of the method of loci, a mnemonic device dating to ancient Greece.

However, in modern cognitive science, it’s more than a trick - spatial structures (like rooms or colours) help the brain encode context boundaries and reduce interference between abstract ideas. Each “room” becomes a mental namespace - effectively, a neural attractor that stabilises related representations while keeping them distinct from others. This aligns with research in working memory and event segmentation: the mind naturally partitions information into episodes with distinct contexts or “boundaries,” making retrieval more efficient.

Mathematicians frequently describe “walking through” a geometric space, “folding” an object in higher dimensions, or “feeling” when something fits or doesn’t. Neuroimaging studies show that visual cortex activity is common when reasoning about geometry or topology, motor cortex can activate when manipulating abstract objects mentally, and prefrontal–hippocampal loops support the maintenance of multiple hypothetical worlds - akin to “rooms” of reasoning. So even though conceptual thought appears detached from the external world, it’s still constructed through embodied metaphors derived from the sensory–motor system.

Assigning colours to theories or ideas (say, “the red space is topology,” “the blue one is category theory”) introduces an affective dimension - a subtle emotional tagging system that helps long-term recall. This parallels how the brain uses valence and salience networks (amygdala, anterior cingulate) to tag memories by importance or feeling. Colour thus becomes both an index (for sorting) and a cue (for recall).

Aspect Real-world perception Conceptual / imagined thought
Input source External sensory data Internal generative model
Neural circuits Shared (sensory, motor, association) Shared (with different weighting)
Signal flow Bottom-up dominant Top-down dominant
Conscious tag “Real” (high confidence, source-marked) “Imagined / abstract” (low confidence)
Function Survival, navigation, action Simulation, planning, abstraction
Example Seeing a path Imagining a path as metaphor for life

Conceptual metaphor theory

Conceptual Metaphor Theory (CMT) is one of the most influential ideas in modern cognitive science and linguistics - and it fundamentally reshapes how we understand abstract thought, memory, and language. Although it sounds like a theory about poetry or language, it actually describes how the human mind structures meaning itself.

At its heart, Conceptual Metaphor Theory (CMT) argues that we understand complex, abstract domains of thought (like time, mathematics, morality, causality, or memory) through mappings from simpler, embodied experiences - things we can see, feel, move through, or act upon. Our concept of time is not purely logical or symbolic - it’s spatialised. We imagine time as a landscape we move through, or as objects moving toward us. CMT is rooted in embodied cognition - the idea that thought arises from bodily experience rather than abstract computation. Our perceptual and motor systems provide the raw material for conceptual structure. Over time, these embodied mappings become invisible - we no longer notice we’re thinking metaphorically.

Bodily schema Conceptual metaphor Example
Vertical orientation GOOD IS UP / BAD IS DOWN “Her mood lifted”; “He fell into depression”
Force dynamics CAUSE IS FORCE “She pushed me to act”; “He resisted change”
Containment STATES ARE CONTAINERS “I’m in love”; “He’s out of trouble”
Path and motion LIFE IS A JOURNEY “He’s come a long way”; “She’s lost her way”

Each conceptual metaphor involves a systematic correspondence:

  • Source domain: concrete experience (e.g., journeys, containers, movement)
  • Target domain: abstract concept (e.g., life, mind, time)
  • Mappings: correspondences between elements of each domain (traveller → person, destination → goal, obstacles → difficulties)

This mapping is partial, not total - only certain features of the source are carried over. That selective structure gives rise to metaphorical reasoning, where logic from the source domain is projected onto the abstract one.

Example:

“He’s stuck in his career”
→ we reason spatially about progress (motion blocked) to describe a conceptual state (lack of advancement).

Lakoff & Núñez (2000) extended this to mathematics, arguing that even mathematics - often seen as pure abstraction - is built from conceptual metaphors grounded in perception:

Mathematical concept Source metaphor
Numbers Collections of objects
Sets Containers
Arithmetic Object manipulation
Functions Machines or paths
Infinity Endless motion or extension

For example, we think of addition as putting objects together and multiplication as repeated addition - both grounded in sensorimotor schemas. This view opposes the Platonic idea that mathematical truths exist independently of the human mind. Instead, mathematics is seen as a human conceptual construction arising from embodied experience.

CMT deeply connects to how memory encodes and retrieves abstract knowledge. Abstract memories (e.g., moral lessons, theories) are often anchored in sensory metaphors (“a dark decision”, “a bright idea”). The method of loci (spatial memory) exploits this principle deliberately - encoding abstract material into spatial form. Conceptual metaphors provide compression: they package large-scale abstract systems into manageable embodied models. Thus, conceptual metaphor is a bridge between experience, language, and conceptual memory - enabling recall not just of facts but of relationships.

Metaphor is not linguistic decoration but a neural re-use mechanism - leveraging old circuits for new conceptual domains. Conceptual metaphors interconnect into large-scale networks. For example:

  • LIFE IS A JOURNEY
  • PURPOSES ARE DESTINATIONS
  • ACTIONS ARE MOTIONS

Together → a whole reasoning system: If you move steadily toward your goals, you make progress in life. This compositional ability may have evolved as an efficient representational strategy: reusing spatial reasoning (ancient and efficient) to manage high-dimensional abstract systems.

While CMT has been transformative, some critiques note that not all abstract thought is metaphorical (some may be relational or diagrammatic). Different cultures may use distinct source domains for the same abstract ideas, and metaphor may be just one layer in a broader system of conceptual blending, where multiple frames combine to create new meaning. Nevertheless, nearly all modern models of meaning - from linguistics to AI semantics - draw upon the embodied, metaphorical nature of cognition.

Summary

Principle Description Example
Embodiment Abstract thought arises from sensory-motor experience “High hopes” (vertical schema)
Mapping Systematic correspondence between domains Journey → Life
Neural reuse Same brain regions reused for abstract reasoning Grasping → Understanding
Conceptual compression Metaphor compresses high-dimensional reasoning into embodied forms “Balance of power”, “Weight of evidence”
Cultural variability Source domains differ across languages Time flows “forward” (English) vs. “downward” (Mandarin)

Simulation

The same neural architecture is used for both real and conceptual experience, but the difference lies in the pattern, strength, and context of activation - not in a completely separate system. When you imagine, remember, or reason conceptually, your brain doesn’t build an entirely new subsystem - it reuses the circuits originally evolved for perception and action. This is known as neural reuse or simulation-based cognition.

  • Visual cortex activates when you imagine or recall an image.
  • Motor cortex activates when you imagine movement.
  • Somatosensory cortex lights up when you empathise with touch or pain.
  • Even olfactory regions activate faintly when you imagine a smell.

So, in conceptual thought, your brain is effectively running an internal simulation of perception - a kind of “as if” mode. This re-use is what allows metaphorical mappings (“grasp an idea,” “see the logic”) to feel natural; the brain activates the same sensorimotor templates that originally handled grasping or seeing.

Although the same circuits are involved, the control hierarchy distinguishes internal simulation from external perception.

Level Function Key structures
Sensory input layer Real sensory data flows in Retinas, cochlea, skin receptors → thalamus → cortex
Simulation layer Internal model generates predicted input Hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, parietal association areas
Comparator / gate Compares prediction vs actual input Anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), posterior parietal, cerebellum

When external sensory data arrives, it overwrites or suppresses the internal simulation (bottom-up dominance). When you’re imagining or thinking, the input gates are partially closed (top-down dominance). You could think of this as a balance of signal sources:

Perception: world → brain (bottom-up)
Imagination/concept: brain → world-model (top-down)

Both use the same architecture; the brain’s predictive coding system simply changes which direction dominates. Within the predictive processing or Free-Energy Principle (Friston) framework, this is understood as a hierarchical generative model. The brain constantly predicts sensory input:

Perception = predictions constrained by sensory data (error correction).
Imagination / thought = predictions run freely with sensory input suppressed.

So the difference is in precision weighting: during perception, prediction error signals (from sensory mismatch) are high-precision and drive updating. During imagination, those error signals are gated down - the model “runs open-loop,” generating its own sensory streams. Dreaming, daydreaming, and conceptual reasoning are therefore variations of the same generative process, with differing levels of sensory constraint.

Experimental evidence

fMRI and EEG studies show high overlap between visual imagery and perception - but imagery tends to activate higher-level association areas more strongly and early sensory areas more weakly. TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) on visual cortex can disrupt both actual vision and imagined images - confirming shared circuitry. In REM sleep, when sensory input is blocked and motor output is inhibited, the brain’s generative model runs almost unconstrained, producing vivid internal “perceptions” (dreams). In waking conceptual thought, the same mechanism is active, but under frontal executive control - we keep the imagined content tethered to logical structure.

Subjective sense of difference

The feeling that “this is real” vs. “this is imagined” emerges from metacognitive tagging - the brain’s ability to track source and confidence of its representations. Hippocampus and prefrontal cortex store contextual markers (time, source, intentionality). If this tagging fails (as in hallucinations or confabulations), imagined content is mistaken for reality. In normal cognition, a constant comparison loop evaluates coherence with sensory data and prior context - our built-in “reality monitor.” So the difference is not in what circuits are used, but in how their output is labelled, constrained, and integrated.

Conceptual thought as attenuated perception

In a sense, conceptual thinking is perception turned inward and downsampled - stripped of raw sensory intensity but retaining the relational geometry of experience.

Process Type Description
Perception High-energy, data-driven Full sensory input dominates predictions
Imagery / memory Balanced Internal model replays prior inputs
Conceptual thought Model-driven Abstraction of relationships without full sensory fidelity

The continuum runs from vivid reality → recollection → abstraction, not as discrete modes but as variable strengths of the same generative engine.

The creative process (e.g. in mathematics, art, philosophy) relies on intentionally shifting between real-world grounding and unconstrained simulation - toggling precision gates. Insight often comes when the top-down model temporarily dominates (imagination free to recombine), followed by a bottom-up check (does it fit reality?). Meditative states and some psychedelics modulate this gating, blending perception and imagination into a unified field - where distinctions blur.
